newsitem.title: USA: Stock investors awaiting latest economic data.
newsitem.headline: Stock investors awaiting latest economic data.

text.p: With first quarter earnings season mostly over, stock investors will be awaiting news on the economy and interest rates next week.
While some companies still have their quarterly reports ahead of them, Wall Street is likely to start fretting about what the Federal Reserve will do when its policy-makers next meet on May 20.
It will be a perfect week to stress out over rates.
Monday brings a report on March new home sales. Tuesday follows with the first quarter Employment Cost Index and April consumer confidence.

The first look at the performance of the overall economy in the first quarter is due Wednesday. The April purchasing manager's report comes Thursday, and Friday brings the eagerly awaited, and dreaded, employment report for April.
"The last big week for earnings is over. Now we revert to a rate-driven market," said Thom Brown, managing director at Rutherford Brown and Catherwood.
On Friday, the Dow Jones industrial average fell 53.38 points to 6,738.87. For the week, the Dow gained 35.32 points.
Brown said investors would be keeping an eye out for any glimmer of inflation in data starting on Monday and that perceptions of inflation will dictate the market's tone.
"Any suggestion that inflation is surfacing will be a negative. Anything that suggests it's not surfacing will be a positive. We're in for a very interest rate-sensitive market," he said.

The market is seeing a tug-of-war between strong earnings reports and the fear of a yield on the 30-year Treasury bond that is already above the 7 percent level, at which bonds start to become more attractive than stocks to some investors.
"We will continue to see good earnings and still have interest rate risks," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter.

"We're in a trading range environment, with the range between 6,300 and 6,800 on the Dow," he said. "I'm not sure we are finished on the upside. I can see us breaking through 6,800, but I doubt we could go above 7,000. In the short-term, we have to see how aggresively the Fed moves in May."
Peggy Farley, chief executive officer at Amas Securities, said that concern about rates was pervading the market and had erased recent gains.
"Whether this fear is predicated on reality or not, I don't know. I tend to think it isn't," she said.

"If I were on the Fed, I'd take a wait and see attitude ... I don't think it's a foregone conclusion that the Fed will raise rates again in May. There is a lot of ammunition to support the argument that inflation has been contained, wages are not surging higher and that the economy is slowing down."
Fed policy-makers raised the federal funds rate, a key short-term rate, a quarter point on March 25, the first time the central bank raised rates in more than two years.

Farley said that high-technology stocks, which have taken a beating despite a rally in shares of International Business Machines Corp. on Thursday after a strong earnings report, were still maong the best sectors in the market.

"I think the high techs are one area that is impervious to the strong dollar in terms of our ability to continue to export," she said. "The techs always fall first because they are vulnerable. There is an aura of speculation about them so the money gets pulled out of them first. But they will continue to show solid earnings."
The meeting of G7 ministers and central bank governors starting this Sunday may also have an impact on markets, said Michael Metz, chief investment strategist at Oppenheimer & Co.

"It's one of the wild cards," Metz said of the meeting. "No one expects anything. But I think they may send a signal that the period of maximum monetary accommodation is behind us. This will have an impact on bonds and, therefore, the stock market.
"We've seen the big bounce back in stocks, partly due to some positive surprises in the earnings reports. Now, I think investors will be more circumspect and cautious."
